summary: Learners organise and count outcomes systematically with Venn diagrams (and two-way tables), reading off unions (A ∪ B), intersections (A ∩ B) and complements (A′). The crux is handling the overlap: elements in both sets belong only in the intersection and are counted once, while elements in neither set still live inside the universal-set rectangle and must be accounted for so all regions total the whole population.
misconceptions: Double-counting the intersection when finding the union (writing |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B|)
Writing each set's full total inside its circle without subtracting the overlap, so the diagram over-counts
Placing elements in the intersection that belong to only one set
Forgetting the 'neither' region, so the regions don't total the whole population

activities.title: Build the Venn and expose the double-count
steps: Use 30 student tokens (physical or on-screen) and a two-circle Venn (A = football, B = cricket) inside a universal rectangle, with the facts: 18 like football, 14 like cricket, 6 like both.

Try the instinctive approach first: allocate 18 to the football circle and 14 to the cricket circle without using the overlap. Those two counts sum to 32 (18 + 14), yet only 30 students exist — on screen a counter reads 32, while with physical tokens you run out before finishing the cricket circle. Either outcome shows that some students are being counted twice — here, the 6 'both' students. Note that the excess of 2 (32 − 30) is not the size of the overlap, because 4 students like neither sport.
Move the 6 'both' students into the overlap region, then adjust so each circle's own-only region reads 12 (18 − 6) and 8 (14 − 6).
Place the 4 left-over students in the 'neither' region inside the rectangle, and check the regions total 30.
State the union count by adding the distinct regions once: 12 + 6 + 8 = 26.
Shade and state in words what each region means for A ∪ B, A ∩ B and A′.
activities.insight: Elements in both sets are counted twice if you compute |A| + |B|; filling the intersection first and subtracting it from each total gives the correct circle-only regions, and the 'neither' region must be included so everything totals the population.

activities.title: Classify, count, and cross-check with a two-way table
steps: Sort each element into its correct Venn region (football-only, cricket-only, both, or neither).
Decide which count is the union of A and B, distinguishing the correct 26 from the double-counted 32.
Give the 'neither' count by reconciling against the total of 30.
Re-represent the same combined events in a two-way / contingency table and check the cell totals match the Venn region counts.
activities.insight: A two-way table is an alternative organiser for combined events; cross-checking it against the Venn diagram confirms every outcome is counted exactly once.

activities.title: Read the regions: tap-to-reveal reference
steps: Study a labelled Venn diagram and tap each region or shaded set to reveal its set notation (for example A ∩ B, or A ∪ B and A′, which are each made of more than one region), its plain-language meaning, and its count.
Match each shaded picture to its correct name and verbal description before building your own diagram.
activities.insight: Fluency with the layout and the meaning of each shaded region supports accurate building and counting.

activities.title: Socratic overlap check
steps: Work through prompts such as 'Does the 18 include the 6 who like both, or not?' and explain your reasoning.
Answer 'How many like football OR cricket, and why isn't it simply 18 + 14?' in your own words.
Explain where the students who like neither go and how many there are.
activities.insight: Articulating why the overlap must be subtracted once, and why the 'neither' group still sits inside the universal set, consolidates the enumeration logic.

checkQuestion: Give the child this and paper: 'In a class of 30, 18 students like football, 14 like cricket, and 6 like both. Draw a two-circle Venn diagram and fill in the numbers. Then shade and give the count for: likes football OR cricket (A ∪ B); likes both (A ∩ B); and does NOT like football (A′).' (Set the task and WATCH — watch whether they subtract the 6 from each circle, whether the union double-counts the overlap, and whether they place the students who like neither.)
checkAnswer: A correct performance: 6 in the intersection, 12 in football-only (18 − 6), 8 in cricket-only (14 − 6), and 30 − (12 + 6 + 8) = 4 outside both circles. A ∪ B = 12 + 6 + 8 = 26 (not 18 + 14 = 32). A ∩ B = 6. A′ (not football) = cricket-only + neither = 8 + 4 = 12. Regions are filled by subtracting the overlap, the union is counted once, and the 'neither' region is included.
